blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
This is our nineteenth show together!
Today we meet two record-breakers.
One will astonish you: he is one hundred and six years old, and he jumps out of planes.
The other is small, round, and furry — and it makes the world's strangest poop.
Ready?
Let's go!

title: 一百零六岁的跳伞爷爷

blocks.en: Meet Al Blaschke from Texas — the world's bravest great-grandpa.
At one hundred and six, Al climbed into a plane, rose nine thousand feet, and jumped out, strapped to an instructor, to win back the record for the oldest tandem skydiver.
Below, his family held their breath.
Then his parachute opened, and the field erupted in cheers.
The media filmed him floating down.
At one hundred and three, he had jumped from fourteen thousand feet for his twin grandsons' graduation — and set the record.
"That was my dream," he said.
But a Swedish grandmother named Rut took the record away.
Al smiled and promised to win it back; the governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, promised to jump beside him.
It was a close shave: bad weather cancelled the jump four times.
Climbing out is awkward work at any age — the service crew checked his straps a dozen times!
At last, a clear morning came.
Al and the governor jumped together, and the record belonged to Al again.
Reporters asked his secret.
"If you think you can't, you are underestimating yourself," he said.
"Everyone is more capable than they think.
They just need to decide to try."
Now shrink down to Australia, to meet the wombat: a round, furry marsupial with short legs.
The wombat's dynasty is ancient — its cousins once included giants as big as a rhinoceros.
Today's wombats are smaller, but they hold a record no other animal can claim: they make cube-shaped poop.
A wombat's intestine is about ten metres long, and a meal may take fourteen days to cross it, growing drier and drier.
Near the end of the tube, the wall is stretchy in some places and stiff in others, so the dry waste is slowly pressed into flat sides and square corners.
Scientists Patricia Yang and David Hu solved the mystery: nobody cuts or moulds the cubes — the intestine squeezes them into shape with tens of thousands of tiny squeezes.
The significance reached far beyond poop: the discovery won a funny science prize, the Ig Nobel Prize.
Why cubes?
Wombats talk by smell.
They stack the cubes on rocks and logs by their burrows, like little flags: "This home is taken!" A cube cannot roll away, and rain cannot easily damage the message.
Here's today's idiom: "down to earth." It describes someone practical, honest, and friendly, who never shows off.

Think of Al: he flies nine thousand feet up, yet stays down to earth, telling everyone, "You can do it too." Here's an example: "Our teacher is really down to earth — she jokes with us and never acts like a star." That's the appeal: simple words for real, honest people.
Let's think about our stories.
A great-grandpa of one hundred and six jumped out of a plane, and a wombat makes perfect cubes.
Now, two questions for you.
First: what brave thing would you like to try when you are very, very old?
Second: if you could leave one special mark on the world, what would it be?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Be brave like Al, stay down to earth like the wombat — and never say "I can't." See you tomorrow morning!
